formulas.name: The balance-sheet identity
formulas.note: Every walkthrough ends here. If it does not balance you have missed a line — nine times out of ten it is retained earnings.

formulas.name: EBITDA from EBIT
formulas.note: Kestrel: EBIT 100 + D&A 20 = £120m. EBITDA is not in the accounts — you build it.

formulas.name: Net income
formulas.note: Kestrel: (100 − 10) × 0.75 = £67.5m. Interest is deducted before tax, which is why debt has a tax shield.

formulas.name: Cash from operations
formulas.note: Start at net income, add back what never moved cash, then adjust for money tied up in working capital.

formulas.name: Free cash flow
formulas.note: The cash actually left over once the business has been kept running.

formulas.name: Net working capital
formulas.note: Operating items only — cash and debt are excluded. An increase is a use of cash.

formulas.name: The working-capital days
formulas.note: Receivables against revenue; inventory and payables against COGS, because that is what they are measured at.

formulas.name: Cash conversion cycle
formulas.note: Days between paying your supplier and being paid by your customer. Negative means suppliers fund your growth.

formulas.name: Tax shield of a non-cash charge
formulas.note: The one line that decides the classic question. A £10m charge at 25 % leaves cash £2.5m higher, not £10m lower.

canonical.q: Walk me through the three statements.
canonical.a: The income statement shows revenue less costs over a period, ending in net income. The balance sheet is a snapshot at one instant: what the company owns on one side, and on the other the liabilities and equity that funded it. Cash flow reconciles net income to the actual change in cash through operating, investing and financing. Net income links the income statement to both the others, and the change in cash closes the loop.

canonical.q: Depreciation goes up by £10m. Walk me through the statements.
canonical.a: At 25 % tax: operating profit falls £10m, tax falls £2.5m, net income falls £7.5m. On the cash flow statement net income is down £7.5m but you add back the £10m non-cash charge, so cash rises £2.5m. On the balance sheet cash is up £2.5m and PP&E is down £10m, so assets fall £7.5m; retained earnings fall £7.5m. It balances.

canonical.q: Which statement would you pick if you could only have one?
canonical.a: The cash flow statement — it shows the cash the business actually generated, which is what services debt and pays shareholders. Net income can be shaped by accounting choices; cash is harder to argue with. The trade-off is losing the profitability picture and the asset base, and seeing only one period.

canonical.q: How can a profitable company go bankrupt?
canonical.a: Because profit is not cash. It can be selling on credit and not collecting, tying cash up in inventory as it grows, spending heavily on capex, or facing a debt repayment it cannot refinance. Profit is recognised when earned; insolvency happens when cash runs out — a fast-growing company with long receivables can be profitable and broke at the same time.

canonical.q: What is working capital and what does an increase mean?
canonical.a: Receivables plus inventory less payables — the operating money tied up in running the business. An increase is a use of cash: you have either let customers pay later or bought stock you have not sold. That is why growth usually consumes cash, and why the cash flow statement subtracts the change in working capital.

traps: Revenue is not cash — a sale on credit adds receivables, not cash.
The balance sheet is a snapshot, not a record of what was earned this year.
Equity is not cash. It is a claim, not a bank balance.
Inventory bought on credit: no income-statement effect at all until it is sold.
Depreciation up means cash **up** by the tax shield — never down by the full charge.
A gain on an asset sale is stripped out of operating cash flow; the whole proceeds sit in investing.
Dividends never touch the income statement — they are a financing outflow and a hit to retained earnings.
An increase in working capital is a use of cash, not a source.
one_liners: Walk IS → CFS → BS, and finish on assets − liabilities − equity = 0.
Non-cash charges cost you profit and save you tax.
Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact.
